column3: Near-verbatim parallel: Noah refuses to expel those who believe, grounding their standing in meeting their Lord.

God's favored community is humble toward believers, supporting a community ethic opposed to elite contempt.
Elites ask whether God favored these people over them, directly exposing the status-based objection behind excluding believers.
The arrogant chiefs question low-status believers about Salih, while those believers affirm his mission despite the hierarchy imposed on them.
The chiefs threaten to expel Shu'ayb and those who believe with him, a direct parallel to coercive exclusion of a believing community.
The chiefs warn that following Shu'ayb will bring loss, directly pressuring people away from the messenger and his believers.
Believing men and women are described as allies of one another, supporting mutual inclusion rather than social sorting.
Mockers ridicule believers both for abundant giving and for their small means, reflecting contempt directed at believers' social position.
God saves Shu'ayb and those who believe with him, a broad parallel to the preservation of a messenger's believing companions.
It commands steadfast company with those who call on their Lord and forbids looking past them for worldly adornment, directly matching the focus's anti-elite stance.
Opponents claim that following guidance with the messenger will cause their removal from the land, explicitly framing belief as socially dangerous.
It gives men and women of faith equal standing through their devotion and reward, not through inherited rank.
It condemns harming believing men and women without cause, supporting protection of believers from hostile social treatment.
The objection that revelation should have gone to a socially great man exposes the same status criterion rejected in the focus.
Human distinction is relocated from tribe and social rank to reverence before God, directly opposing hierarchical dismissal of believers.
Later believers ask to be cleansed of rancor toward fellow believers, supporting a community that does not reject its members.
The hypocrites urge withholding support from those with the Messenger so they disperse, an explicit attempted exclusion of the believing community.
The claim that the mighty will expel the humbler exposes the same elite logic of removing those deemed socially inferior.
The rebuke begins when attention turns away from a disadvantaged seeker, directly challenging preference for elite audiences.
The blind man who approaches becomes the concrete counterpoint to status-based neglect of a sincere believer.
His possible purification establishes that spiritual receptivity, not social standing, governs whom the messenger should attend.
The possibility that remembrance benefits him reinforces priority for the receptive seeker over the prestigious rejecter.
The self-sufficient elite is explicitly contrasted with the needy seeker, exposing the social preference corrected by the passage.
Giving full attention to the self-sufficient person directly contrasts with the focus's refusal to accommodate elite demands.
The messenger is not accountable for an elite rejecter's failure to purify himself, limiting accommodation of statusful opponents.
The earnest seeker is defined by his coming with effort, grounding his claim on responsiveness rather than rank.
His reverent fear marks the quality that outweighs the elite's worldly self-sufficiency.
Turning away from the striving, reverent seeker is the precise reversal of the posture affirmed in the focus.
Criminals laugh at believers, a direct example of hostile social contempt toward the faithful.
Their mocking gestures when believers pass portray sustained public humiliation of the faithful.
The mockers return to their own circle amused, showing elite-group reinforcement of contempt for believers.
They label believers as astray, directly echoing the presumptuous social judgment rejected by the focus.
The command not to repel one who asks supplies a broad ethical parallel to refusing to drive away the vulnerable.
